questions.prompt: Which mode must JMeter use in a CI pipeline?
options: Non-GUI (-n)
GUI
Remote GUI
Recorder mode
questions.explanation: CI agents have no display and need the lightweight CLI mode.

questions.prompt: Which file produced by the HTML report is easiest for a script to read pass/fail numbers from?
options: statistics.json in the report folder
index.html
jmeter.log
The .jmx
questions.explanation: statistics.json has per-label metrics such as errorPct and pct1ResTime in machine-readable form.

questions.prompt: JMeter's exit code is non-zero by default when some samples fail.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: JMeter exits 0 when the run completes, even with failed samples, so the pipeline needs its own gate (script, plugin or tool).

questions.prompt: Which load test belongs on every merge request?
options: A short smoke-load test (few users, a few minutes) with a strict error gate
A 4-hour soak test
A full peak test with 10,000 users
No performance test at all
questions.explanation: Short runs give quick feedback; long or heavy tests run nightly or before releases.

questions.prompt: Why should CI performance runs use a dedicated, stable environment?
options: Shared, noisy environments make results vary run to run, causing false failures and missed regressions
Because JMeter only runs on dedicated servers
To avoid generating an HTML report
Because CI cannot reach shared environments
questions.explanation: Variance hides real changes. JMeter itself runs anywhere.

questions.prompt: Which are good pipeline steps? Select all that apply.
options: Pin the JMeter version (e.g. a container image) and install required plugins in the build
Archive the JTL and HTML report as build artefacts
Fail the job when thresholds are breached
Store credentials in the .jmx committed to Git
questions.explanation: Reproducible tooling, artefacts and gates make CI tests useful. Credentials belong in the CI secret store passed via -J properties.

questions.prompt: A gate script reads this from statistics.json. Thresholds: errorPct <= 1 and pct3ResTime (p99 by default) <= 1500. Which outcome is right?
options: Fail, because errorPct 1.2 exceeds 1 even though the p99 passes
Pass, both are within limits
Fail, because pct3ResTime is the p90
Pass, because errorPct is rounded down
questions.explanation: 1.2 > 1 fails the error gate. With default report settings pct1/pct2/pct3 are p90/p95/p99, so 1400 is the p99 and passes. No rounding applies.

questions.prompt: The CI job passes, but the published report shows 100% errors. The gate script reads `statistics.json['total']`. What is wrong?
options: The key is 'Total' (capital T); the script probably defaults to 0 when the key is missing, so it never fails. Fail the gate when expected data is missing
statistics.json is not produced in CI
JMeter's exit code should have failed it
The report is wrong in CI
questions.explanation: A missing key that silently becomes 0 makes a gate useless. Gates must fail closed. JMeter's exit code does not reflect sample errors.

coding.title: A fail-closed CI gate
coding.prompt:
Write `gate(stats, max_error_pct, max_p95_ms)` where `stats` is the parsed `statistics.json` dict. Use the `'Total'` entry's `errorPct` and `pct2ResTime` (p95 with default settings). Return `(passed, reasons)`:

- reason `'error rate'` if errorPct > max, `'p95'` if pct2ResTime > max;
- if `'Total'` is missing, or `sampleCount` is 0/missing, return `(False, ['no data'])` (fail closed).

Example: `{'Total': {'sampleCount': 10, 'errorPct': 0, 'pct2ResTime': 300}}` with (1, 500) returns `(True, [])`.
coding.explanation: Fail-closed defaults (100% errors, infinite p95, 'no data') mean a broken run or renamed key can never pass by accident.
hints: Use pessimistic defaults for missing metrics.

tests.name: Fail closed
tests.code:
assert gate({'total': {'sampleCount': 10}}, 1, 500) == (False, ['no data'])
assert gate({'Total': {'sampleCount': 0}}, 1, 500) == (False, ['no data'])

coding.title: Build the CI command
coding.prompt:
Write `jmeter_cmd(plan, results, report, props)` returning the argument list for a non-GUI run that writes results, generates the report, and passes each property in `props` (a dict) as `-Jname=value`, sorted by name.

Example: `jmeter_cmd('plan.jmx', 'r.jtl', 'out', {'threads': 5})` returns `['jmeter', '-n', '-t', 'plan.jmx', '-l', 'r.jtl', '-e', '-o', 'out', '-Jthreads=5']`.
coding.solution:
def jmeter_cmd(plan, results, report, props):
    cmd = ['jmeter', '-n', '-t', plan, '-l', results, '-e', '-o', report]
    cmd += [f'-J{k}={props[k]}' for k in sorted(props)]
    return cmd
coding.explanation: Building the command as a list (not a string) avoids shell-quoting bugs, and sorting the properties makes the command reproducible in logs.
hints: Sort property names for a stable order.
